utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to greet today Mr. Praljak, Mr. Prlic, and Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. I wouldn't like to forget to greet those who are absent as well. I would also like to greet Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer and his assistants, and everyone else assisting us in the courtroom. One administrative announcement I would first like to make. As the Gotovina Chamber won't be sitting tomorrow morning, tomorrow, the hearing will be held in the morning instead of in the afternoon. So we will start with the hearing tomorrow morning. I, personally, I think this is also the opinion of others, prefer the morning. I know that Mr. Praljak prefers to have lunch first, but it will be necessary for him to have a substantial breakfast on this occasion. However the case may be, we will be sitting tomorrow morning. Next week, there will be the appointment of new Judges. There's a former lawyer among them, there are rumours to that effect, or there has been rumours to that effect, for sure. These Judges will be taking their oath on the 2nd of December [as interpreted] in this courtroom, and as a result we will have to complete our hearing at 1.00 p.m. and not at 1.45. So the hearing will end at 1.00 p.m. because they need one hour to prepare the courtroom to place the Judges here. So as they will be taking their oath at 2.00 p.m., it will be necessary for us to end at 1.00 p.m. That's what I wanted to inform you of. Mr. Stringer, I'd like to greet you once again. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I thought you had completed what you wanted to say. Perhaps towards the end of the day, I could be granted a few minutes so that I could make sure we all have the same information with regard to our schedule for our forthcoming witnesses, the witnesses who will be testifying after Mr. Praljak, because I can foresee certain scheduling problems and I'd like to spend a few minutes on this matter later on. Mr. Stringer and myself have been exchanging information to that effect, but nevertheless ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes, would you need about ten minutes, so we could end ten minutes earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I need a few minutes, but I don't know to what extent others will be taking the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. In fact, I was concerned about this matter as well, so it would be good if you informed us of any problems that you might encounter. Mr. Stringer, I greet you once again and I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone else in and around the courtroom. Mr. President, I hate to say this, but it turns out that I've got a personal matter scheduled for tomorrow morning, and we do have lives outside of this trial and this courtroom that we have to arrange around the court hours. If I could maybe just have some time to sort of think about it over the break and see if perhaps I can find a way to accommodate things. I'd at least like to have the possibility to come back to the Trial Chamber later today about the situation. I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I see that you do not have the binder that we were working with yesterday, so I'll ask that the usher provide that to you. This is the list number 6 of documents. And the next exhibit, General, as we continue talking about Prozor is Exhibit P00640 [realtime transcript read in error "P00460"]. General, do you want to take a moment to look that document over? This is a list of -- I believe it's prepared by the SDA of Prozor municipality. It's entitled "List of Vehicles Confiscated in Prozor Municipality Since the HVO and HV Aggression Begun ...," in other words, from 23 October, 1993. Now, General, I know that you subsequently to this date of 23 October -- oh, Mr. President, I'm told the document is under seal and that we need to go into private session for this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Praljak, I'd like to go back to the issues of the vehicles. First of all, and this is something you have pointed out, there were three vehicles that belonged to the ABiH, so they could be considered as falling under the category of war booty. Perhaps you noted, but perhaps you didn't have the time, that in fact there were 161 individuals concerned, because the five vehicles that were confiscated in August, not on the 24th of October, but on the 20th of August. It's in the list, and then there were individuals who had or owned a number of vehicles. But this isn't what my question relates to. It seems that there might be three situations, three possible situations: war booty; legitimate confiscation by an army, with receipts delivered and the signature of the owner; and, thirdly, the theft, pure and simple, of vehicles by X, Y, or Z. At the level of the HVO, did you consider these various cases, these various situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the HVO, a vehicle could be commandeered for war needs in certain situations, but then a receipt would be issued to the owner. It would contain information on the make of the car, the date of the car, and so on and so forth. And on the base of the receipt or signatures issued to him, the owner could then request that the vehicle be returned to him or that he be compensated for the damage, and so on and so forth. Naturally, there was also the case of classical or traditional war booty. The enemy unit fled and left equipment of any kind, military equipment or a car, well, then naturally that would be listed as war booty for the unit concerned. And naturally there were cases of theft, too. All I can say is that I very much doubt that the number of cars was so high, as I doubt that they were attacked by the HV, and in any war there's a lot of propaganda. You want to tarnish the reputation of the other side. But I participated in taking away a vehicle from someone who had stolen a vehicle. A witness testified to that effect here. My pistol was drawn, as in the usual Wild West films, so whoever has better nerves is the person who is victorious, usually. But apart from the HVO, there was a wild HOS unit, a savage HOS unit. Their members were quite numerous. It was difficult to control them, impossible to control them. I made many attempts to control the situation. It's too long to explain, this story is too long to explain. They weren't under control, and a lot of time passed before they left the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to make sure, on line 21 -- 20-21, you are reported as saying: "... that I very much doubt, that the number of cars was so high, as I doubt that they were attacked by the HV ..." Just to make sure, you wanted to say "HV" and not "HVO" here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. They say in the document that an aggression was conducted against them by the HVO and the HV, which is simply false, it's a lie. Let me be quite frank about it. And then one lie follows another, and they are accumulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't see the link to any other lies, but this I take. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit in your binder is P00662 [realtime transcript read in error "P06622"], 6622. Now, this is a document dated 28 October 1992. It's signed for Ilija Franjic, and, General, is it correct that this is the same Ilija Franjic that we talked about yesterday on the list of people who were appointed to positions in the municipal HVO of Prozor by Mate Boban in the document that was signed for him by Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, with a high degree of certainty, yes, but I can't tell you 100 per cent. I do know one Ilija Franjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the Ilija Franjic that you know, was he a brigade commander of the Rama Brigade, as is indicated in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was in Rama, he was commander of the Rama Brigade. At the time of this event, he was brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Again, the number, P00662 is the number of the document, as I see it. In the record, line 21 of page 13, it says, wrongly, "P06622." So the correct number would be P00662.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to be more -- I think I got that one right, but if I didn't, I'll be more careful with the next ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No criticism here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, now this one is dated the 28th of October. Were you in Prozor by the 28th of October, again if our reference is that Jajce fell on or about that day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is highly, highly probable that on the 28th of October, I was in Rama. A day later, perhaps, or a day earlier. And then I went to Konjic, Jablanica. Mr. Stringer, I'm trying -- I was moving around from one meeting to another, but I simply am unable to say exactly that on that particular day I was in Rama. I didn't keep any notes, nor did I have any time to do that. And though I'm doing my best, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in this document the commander of the Rama Brigade is ordering the release of some prisoners who were being held at a place called Ripci so that they can be used to load MTS. General, during this period of time, recognising that you were in Prozor, but that you were moving elsewhere as well, were you aware of the presence of HVO prisoners at a place called Ripci?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it says "detainees" and not "prisoners." I think there's a difference there. That's number 1. And, number 2, it is true that when I learnt that there were detainees as a result of this conflict, I asked, and my request was met, that they should all be released, and they were released. Now, whether this was on the 29th or the 30th, I can't tell you exactly, but I insisted and requested, and my request was met and they were all sent home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did you request that they be released because they were -- there were no proper grounds for holding them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. I had the people who were opposed to such a position, and quite logically, actually. And on the basis of the documents confiscated by the HVO, it was clear that these members of the ABiH army were preparing an attack. They had detailed plans as to how and when they would attack. These people needed to be interrogated and, if there was a basis, then processed. However, as it was far more important at that point in time to deal with the situation, I requested that all this be put aside, that people be sent home so that confidence could be rebuilt, because the common enemy had already captured Jajce, and according to my knowledge there was no good defence between Travnik and Sarajevo. So in view of such a situation, the people had to be sent home and the situation dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to this detention facility and see any of the people who were being held there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go there. But immediately after that, I spoke to their commander, Zutic or something like that, that was his name, that he should go and see his people, that we should have another meeting, that the elders of the village should come, and so on and so on. It was all very complicated, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, and I know that you're using the word "request," the fact is that as an assistant minister of defence for the Republic of Croatia and as someone who is at this time a major general in the Croatian Army, the fact is that whether you call it a request or an order, the fact is that your authority is the reason why those people were released when you wanted them released; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, if someone were to send an assistant minister from Zagreb, that simply is not true. As you saw in the case of the humanitarian convoy that was stopped at Citluk, a representative of the international community spoke, the former minister of Croatia, Granic, and Prlic, and they wouldn't listen to them. So my authority at that time emanated from the fact that I had certain successes, in the military sense, in liberating Mostar and halting the Army of Republika Srpska and the Yugoslav Army in the spring and summer of 1992, and not simply because somebody may have sent someone from Zagreb to be -- or hand out wise advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that based on your prior experience and military activities in other theaters of battle, they recognised your authority and they did what you told them to do; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I think I know how to talk to people. I can talk to them passionately, I don't lie to them, and I think that is the basis on account of which they listened to me, nothing else, and the fact that I explained to them that Central Bosnia would fall, that we have to calm down, that units have to head towards Travnik to save that, and so on and so forth. I think the Muslims trusted me, too, and you saw this from the witnesses, because I wasn't partial. I treated both Croats and Muslims equally. I didn't lie to them. I told them the facts, I told them what could be done, I told them that things could not be resolved overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And based on all of these things, then, General, that you're telling us, the HVO in Prozor at this time recognised your authority, and they did what you told them to do, correct, for all the reasons that you've been giving us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a request, and they acted upon it. Now, why they did that, I wouldn't like to enter into that. I don't know. You can call them and ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to take you back to the testimony of Mr. Hujdur, Omer Hujdur, who we talked about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems, Mr. Stringer, that you are leaving this document and this issue of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm leaving the document, but not the issue of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Anyway, I would like to ask two questions, raise two points. The first is, and I think I know the answer, but I would like to hear it from you, anyway: How many prisoners were there at that moment, 28 October 1992, in Ripci, how many detained persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That is, in fact, the answer that I expected. The second point is: You seem to read this document as some sort of evidence that you had persons who had been detained in the context of operations in Prozor released in order to reconcile things and so forth. I find it not easy to reconcile this document with such a thesis, because this does not say that the prisoners were to be released to go home, but they were to be released and put at the disposal of Ante Simunovic, I'm quoting, "for loading MTS." So this might even be similar to what we have seen with prisoners from Heliodrom, to take but one example, where prisoners are taken and then put to work somewhere. I'm not commenting whether that would have been the work and putting them to work in this way would have been or not in conformity with the 3rd, I think, Geneva Conventions, but why should we suppose that these people were really left to go home, or did I misunderstand you, that you were saying that your intervention had the scope of letting them go home and be really free.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, the release came after this. There's no doubt at all that there were detainees and members of the ABiH who were detained, and that they considered themselves detainees. And someone here asked them to load MTS, which I think is permissible. It's not up to me to judge. But I do know that I released them all home; not I, but I asked that they all be released, and they were released. So this must have been before my request and before my request was heeded, so that is the time sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That would lead me, then -- thank you. That would lead me, then, to conclude that this document actually is practically irrelevant. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what is it relevant for. That there were detainees? Of course there were detainees. Who would I release if there weren't any detainees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'm going to move on to another area which has nothing to do with prisoners. I'm looking at the document, and I'm going to compare this document which is in your binder, P1327, but for the moment let's keep to this document. What do I see: "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Prozor Municipality, Rama Brigade," and then a number. And reading this document by a strict jurist would lead to the conclusion that the person issuing the order is, in fact, a part of the Rama municipality and that the Rama Brigade is a municipal brigade with a military task, but certainly municipal. Why? Because it doesn't say "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" in the heading, and also it doesn't say the "Croatian Defence Council." Now, when we look at document P1327 - could the Registrar find it, please - look at this document, please. I want to see the header. You see a change there. Here, we have the words "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," then the "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," and unlike the previous document, "Croatian Defence Council" and "Command of the Rama Brigade." And this is a document from January, and the other is from October. On that basis, I am asking the following question, and that is why I'm asking you this: In October, what we qualified as the HVO, were they not forces of a municipal origin and after the events when the Croatian Defence Council took control and militarised these units, which would explain that this document is of an absolutely military nature, which is not the case with the number appearing on the previous document? So the people who were at Prozor, some belonging to the HOS, was this an armed force under municipal control, or the people who were in Prozor, were they directly linked by a chain of command to General Petkovic, who was the military commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The worst thing, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, is that one could say both. They were a municipal force, but the HVO and the Main Staff endeavoured to put it all under military control, and unfortunately this varied. At the beginning, they were more municipal, but then gradually more order would be put into it. Then, due to lack of funds or some other reason, they would return to the control -- municipal control, and again it's not the same for every brigade. For instance, the Livno Brigade was more its own than the Ljubuski Brigade, so the situation varied. The influence of the municipality and the influence borne by the Main Staff varied. There's no equation that can be put between municipalities, between brigades, and also things changed in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But for Prozor, who had more control, the municipality over the military or the military over the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think at this point in time, the municipality was more important than General Petkovic's command and order that the conflict should be calmed down. Such an order coming from the chief of staff over there didn't have too much impact. One could just go there, and with the force of one's will, personality, shouting, ability to deal with people, you could achieve something. But an order, in the military sense, you send an order and it has to be carried out, that didn't function. Not even Siljeg could achieve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the fact that I note that in the month of January the documents change in nature, does this show that the military structure of the HVO had greater control over these brigades then? Because here we have a document which is fully in accord with military criteria.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure about that. There is mention of the Croatian Defence Council. I don't know Simun Zutic, who is the signatory. All I can say is that 11 commanders of the Rama Brigade changed, for various reasons. Two were killed, I think, and the others were replaced in an effort to be more successful, up until Ante Pavelic, who was there, whom I brought from the Croatian Army to try and influence the situation, because the influence of villages and clans, local clans, is very difficult in relation to what we call the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to follow up on the last question from Judge Antonetti, let's turn back to P00647, which is one of the documents we looked at yesterday; 647. This is dated October 24, 1992, so it's a few days earlier. Do you have 647?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this one is the report written by Jure Smidt, the gentleman you smoke about yesterday, and here he's reporting directly to Colonel Siljeg. Now, is it true that at this period of time, the 24th of October, 1992, the Rama Brigade was a part of the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone, which was under the command of Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just follow up my question and then you can comment. So what we're seeing in this document, then, is a report from a member of the Rama Brigade up to the operative zone commander, and there's nothing particularly unusual or remarkable about that reporting chain of command, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. The Jure Smidt says "Commander." It doesn't say what he's commander of. As far as I know, he was not commander of anything in Rama, and yesterday I found a document, a report sent to General Petkovic, which was obviously copied by Jure Smidt, so a report sent to General Petkovic which Jure Smidt copied out and sent to Siljeg. Of what he was commander, I'm sure of nothing in Rama. So obviously he's copied a report here where there's no mention of ethnic cleansing, but a completely different word is used, and he sent something to Siljeg. He's not the commander of a brigade or a battalion or anything in Rama. I don't know what exactly he was doing, but he certainly didn't have a command position in Rama.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, this tells us that a member -- a commander, as is indicated here - and I know you challenge his position - of the Rama Brigade is reporting directly to the commander of the operative zone; isn't that what this tells us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true that that is what the report says, but I don't know what position he held to write that report. He obviously did this at his own initiative. I'm quite certain that in Rama, he didn't have any position, because I would rally those people together and speak to them at least ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to go back to my outline now and recall some of the testimony from an earlier witness in this case, Omer Hujdur, who came and testified about the events in Prozor during October of 1992. And specifically on the 20th of June, 2006, at page 3520 of the transcript, he gives us the following testimony about events that followed in the wake of the military operations in Prozor. It's page 3520, and I think we can put it up on sanction, on line 17. He's asked a question about whether a lot of the people did, indeed, go back to Prozor after the conflict there. He's asked about whether a lot of Bosniaks returned to Prozor who had left, and Hujdur says: "Yes, but this is was some 10 or 11 days later when, probably at some high level, but to this day I don't know at what level and with whom, an agreement was reached that the population should be allowed to go back to Prozor. But terrible things had happened in the town of Prozor itself. Over 70 houses, Bosniak houses, were torched, houses belonging to the more prosperous Bosniaks. About ten civilians were killed as a result of the entry into and conquest of the town. "All the homes and houses that had been left empty because the population had been moved to a safer part of town were looted." It continues on on the next page: "All vehicles were stolen. All the private businesses were destroyed. In these 10 to 11 days, there was intense destructive activity in the town, destruction of property. And after a certain period of time, the people at the high level said that the population should go back. However, it's important to say that the men were separated from the women, and the men were taken to the Ripci primary school, which is 12 kilometres to the west of Prozor, and there all the men had to sign statements to the effect that everything that had happened in Prozor had happened as a result of Bosnian extremists and that they were to blame for this." Now, General, you arrived and you were in the Prozor region during this period of time, some 10 to 11 days after the conflict occurred there. His description of the destruction and the crimes that occurred in Prozor after the HVO took the town, it's an accurate description, isn't it? These are the things that you saw, when you were there, that were taking place; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the way described here by a man who fled from Rama. He cannot know what was going on in Rama. Ten dead civilians, there weren't. That is not true. There are documents signed by both parties on the number of soldiers killed and the rest, and you will see from those numbers that this was a conflict between more or less equal forces, because there was roughly an equal number of casualties on both sides, six or seven on the Bosnian side and four or five on the HVO. And then he says a part of the town, not the whole town, was occupied, and for 10 or 11 days it was necessary -- that time was necessary for the situation to be calmed down. I never heard of such a statement being signed in prison. And that the people who were sent back, that they should be detained, that was absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You are aware, General, that as he indicates here, scores of houses of Muslims, Bosniaks, were torched and were looted after they had fled and after the HVO took the town; that is a true statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. From the time that I arrived up there, there was no more torching, for certain, no more destruction, nothing that could be attributed to the HVO. As to what happened in the course of the fighting itself, well, it certainly has nothing to do with the number referred to by this gentleman. That is completely erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting to you, General, that in fact the damage -- the destruction that he's talking about here is not collateral damage; that this was damage that was inflicted deliberately by HVO soldiers after they'd taken the town, after the military conflict was completed. Isn't that what happened? And you were there while it was happening; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, according to all the information I had, this information was incorrect, and that concerns the ten individuals. That was a lie. You need to have the first and last names. And then to use such numbers and say there were ten of them and tons of houses were torched, that's wrong. I won't claim that there weren't units such as the HOS units that were out of control. I won't say that they didn't do anything. But it is necessary to be quite precise about this. The HVO up there, after the completion of the action, didn't do anything that could be considered as a dishonourable military act. And when I arrived in Rama, a group was roasting some lamb on the spit, raising a flag. I tried to oppose them, and that didn't go well, but I managed to solve the situation on the following day, but in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I want to take you now to some other testimony, the testimony of the "Guardian" journalist, Edward Vulliamy, who testified on the 8th of August, 2006, about what he observed when he drove into Prozor in late 19 -- late October 1992. This would be page 1534 of the transcript. And I'm not going to read all of it, General. I'm going to put it on the screen. I know that it's not in your language. I'll read parts of it to you. He's talking about when they were driving towards Prozor. He says, and this is on line 6: "... but before we got to Prozor, on the junction we saw some women straggling - it was raining - up a road turning off to the left, and stopped to talk to them." And I'm going to skip down a few lines, where he talks about that it was late morning. And then he's asked to describe what happened when he encountered these women walking along, and he says, on line 18: "Yes. We asked them what happened. One of them, I noticed, was wearing bedroom slippers. They looked frightened, they looked bedraggled, and one of them said that they'd spent the night looking for caves, that soldiers were out killing people and looking for them. And as we were having this conversation, a mini-cab pulled up." And he goes on, General, in his testimony, and I'm not going to read it all, to talk about how he, Mr. Vulliamy, and the person who was driving this cab gave these women a ride, and he continues and he says: "A little way up this road and then turning off to the right up a track mountain track, and the track rose up through, I think, some wooded country and then opened out into open country, and there was this amazing sight of large numbers of people wandering the fields in groups or standing, looking to get away, looking for somewhere. I don't know what they were looking for. They were wandering the open country." And he goes on in his testimony to estimate, with difficulty, that it was scores if not hundreds of people that he saw, and he said that they were wandering in the direction of Jablanica. Now, General, recognising that we don't know the exact date and time that Mr. Vulliamy encountered this group of people, General, you wouldn't dispute this testimony, I take it. You don't dispute that there were large numbers of Muslims who were trying to make their way down to Jablanica in the wake of the conflict in Prozor; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, as a child who, from the age of six to ten, lived in Rama, well, I used that road from Rama to Jablanica, I went down that road. Because it was iced over in the winter, I would use a sled to go down there. There are no -- there are no fields there, no fields that can be seen. This man doesn't know what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you dispute -- you don't accept his testimony? You deny that there were hundreds of people out there, as he described, on the road making their way down to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, if a journalist says something like that, there are no fields there, there's just a precipice to the left and a precipice to the right, and the Murgere [phoen] Italian Division came to harm there in the Second World War. They were thrown into the ravine. So if this journalist is saying that he saw a field there, he's lying. There is no field there. You can't turn either to the left or to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Earlier today, General, you've told us about the Muslims whom you met in Jablanica, who had come down there after the conflict in Prozor. So the fact is, as you've already indicated, there were large numbers of Muslims on the move, trying to make their way to Jablanica from Prozor; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you very precisely. The people had fled from Rama -- some of them had fled from Rama and arrived in Jablanica. I spoke to them. But that doesn't mean that there were fields there, and -- and what this gentleman has described is something that doesn't exist. You don't have anything of that kind on that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, if we admit that what you are saying is true and that there are no fields, there is no field, very well, I don't know. If the journalist says that or he said that when he was sitting in your place, well, he said that, but one should bear in mind the fact that he was remembering everything that happened 15 years ago. It's very difficult. I'm sure the journalist saw many things. Perhaps he was confused, he mixed up the road with a field, but nevertheless there's something that is important. He says that he saw Muslims, columns of Muslims, and these people were heading in the direction of Jablanica, and this is what is important. This is what needs to be explained to us. Why were these people heading in the direction of Jablanica? There could be two reasons for this. Either they were forced to do that or they were afraid and, as a result, set off in that direction. You said, I spoke to them in Jablanica. What did they tell you? You should tell us about this, rather than dispute the existence of the field. It's as if you, 15 years later, were to talk about the hearing that is taking place today, and you might say that Mr. Scott was present, but he's not present. So there we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the people I spoke to in Jablanica, well, in the hall there were perhaps between 80 and 100 individuals who had arrived from Rama. They've told me precisely what I have told you: that they had been attacked, that there was fighting, that they had fled. And we spoke about the matter for two or three hours in this manner. But many villages from Jablanica to Rama are Muslim villages, and you saw in the report the HVO was up at -- was as far as Jasen, and then further on the area was under the control of the ABiH. As far as Jasen, the village, the dam, there are no fields. There's just a precipice to the left and to the right. I don't know what the gentleman saw over there, but there are no fields. It's a fact that the soldiers who lost or fled, those who had arms, those who didn't, people were certainly afraid. There were people who had been captured or were being held in detention. The reports show that in many villages the Muslims said, Fine, we'll surrender our weapons, but please leave us in peace. And that is what happened. The first thing doesn't exclude the other. I'm not saying that -- well, I can't exclude all the details, but I'm telling you about the information I had. There was a fight, a conflict. People were detained or released, people returned. There were dead on both sides. We know the precise numbers. There were houses that were damaged, for sure. There were houses that were torched. As to what was done in the course of the fighting, well, the numbers that these people have provided are incorrect. Later, very precise lists were compiled, precise information; each person who was dead, the side the person belonged to, the first and last name. We needed to have a list of the houses so that we could know where shooting was opened from, whether ABiH had machine-gun nests, and the whole town hadn't been conquered. Part of the town was still under the control of the ABiH. This wasn't an attempt to expel the Muslims. There are certainly always individuals who will try to do certain things that violate international -- the International Law of War, International Humanitarian Law, any kind of law, but these are completely different matters; two entirely different matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just for one second, and here is where I believe that there is some confusion at times. When the Prosecution reads from a transcript, where there are numerous facts in a particular passage, and then requests a yes-or-no answer, it requires the person who's answering the question -- if the answer is "yes," it has to be "yes" to all the facts, "no" to all the facts. Yesterday, there was quite a good observation by Judge Trechsel when there was a compound question. The answer was, you know, is it "yes" to the first part, to the second part, to both parts. The record wouldn't reflect that. I believe General Praljak was attempting to answer the question by at least looking at one part of the facts within that passage that he believed was in error. So I think the better approach might be to have questions that are much more focused. I think when the Prosecutor came back on the follow-up question, he got to the essence of the question that he wanted to ask, but the way it was couched the first time, where people are in the fields, wandering about, and so on and so forth, the general was trying to make an observation, and that's why I believe if we're going to, you know, sojourn on through this particular cross-examination, we'll only going to get through it if the questions are much more focused and fact oriented. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to skip over a few pages. I'm going to stay with the testimony of Mr. Vulliamy for just a couple more minutes, because on page 1539 of his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, it would assist us in finding the place in our transcripts if you could indicate the date of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the 8th of May, 2006, and it's now at page 1539, starting on line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He's talking about when they were trying to file their story, and they were heading for a telephone which was in Tomislavgrad, and they reached Tomislavgrad, and it was in Tomislavgrad that Mr. Vulliamy then had the meeting or a meeting with Colonel Siljeg, and I'd like to ask you a few questions about that. And you may or may not recall this testimony, General. Vulliamy spoke about a dinner he had with Colonel Siljeg, and so he is asked to recall the details of his long conversation with Siljeg. And this is what Vulliamy says at page 1540, line 6. He says: "I can recall a few details. Well, I can recall one important detail. He said that Prozor was now clean. He made a reference to the -- the rather drunken celebrations outside as night games, as boys will sort of way. And then he got out a -- he got out a series of maps of Croatia down the centuries, 1 to 12, as I recall, arduously went through each map as Croatia expanded and shrunk, and the last one I remember was labelled "Future Croatian Federation," and had Croatia extending all the way almost to Belgrade and to a place called Zume. And it was the 1941 so-called Banovina Croatia. That was not actually HVO policy at all. It was, if anything, that of its old rival HOS. But it was a long, long lecture about history, as one had got quite used to." General, the -- Colonel Siljeg -- and I'm going to use this to ask you a couple of questions about Colonel Siljeg. You were with him there in the Prozor-Tomislavgrad during late October of 1993, upon your arrival there, and, as I understand, you stayed largely in that area, including Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, and other places, until just before Christmas 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So throughout that period of time, almost two months, you were present and working on a frequent basis in the Siljeg operative zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would meet, but not really that frequently. Work in the operative zone? I didn't really work that frequently in the operative zone, to be quite frank. But I'd be interested in knowing which direction Vulliamy came from and then went to Tomislavgrad. It would be good to see this in the transcript, if it's there, to see if there was anything he could see in the direction of Jablanica, because if he came from Makljen and then turned off towards Tomislavgrad, well, that's in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, your counsel can ask you questions about that when you have your redirect exam. Staying will Colonel Siljeg and the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone, you've indicated already in your testimony that during August and September of 1993, after you took command of the HVO Main Staff, you also spent a good deal of your time then in the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And yesterday we spoke briefly about the division of labour, as we're calling it, that was in place as between yourself and General Petkovic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Registrar, could you please leave the document on the screen, the Vulliamy testimony, where he speaks about Colonel Siljeg, because it's not there anymore and I had a question I wanted to put. I do apologise for interrupting you. Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stringer has reminded us of what the journalist said before us, and he has shown us this document in English. You don't know English, but that's not what is at stake. As far as I understand the matter, Vulliamy says he had a lengthy conversation with Siljeg, and apparently Colonel Siljeg gave him a lesson in history on Croatia and showed him maps, et cetera. And as far as the journalist can remember, he saw a map apparently entitled "Future Croatian Federation." And in line 14, I see that the journalist said that it was not actually HVO policy at all, but rather it was the policy of its old rival, the HOS, and this appears important to me. There was a conversation between Siljeg and Vulliamy. Siljeg showed him some maps, and then one might perhaps have the impression that Siljeg was in favour of this Greater Croatia. He showed him maps, something on the federation, but then the journalist gives his own personal assessment. He has other information at his disposal, and he says that, Siljeg, it's not HVO policy, it's HOS policy. When I see this on the screen, I tell myself, well, perhaps matters are more complicated than one might believe. Siljeg was perhaps passing off personal ideas of his own, or HOS ideas, but ideas which, according to the journalist, were not HVO ideas. You, who know Siljeg, would you say that this is possible or not? How is it that a colonel in the operations zone, who has other things to deal with, has an entire series of maps, historical and other maps? How is it that he has said this? If the journalist said this under oath, so we can assume that this is the truth, there's no reason to think that he said anything else, apparently his memory is quite precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when someone says something under oath, it doesn't mean that he's lying. But as to whether his memory is reliable with regard to his conversation with Siljeg, well, I'm afraid that that might not be true. Siljeg was not conducting HVO policies. He was a military policeman in the JNA. I think he was a major; perhaps he had that rank. He was a professional. As to whether he showed this gentleman how history in the Balkans developed, whether he showed how conquests took place with ten significant forces, I don't know, but Siljeg wasn't in charge of policies and he couldn't say to Vulliamy that Prozor had been cleansed for the simple reason that those who had left -- out of those who had left, 90 per cent of them returned also as a result of attempts made by Mr. Siljeg. So this would contradict any logic. As far as I know, from people who came from the outside, they want to understand the history of a certain area in two days' time. As a rule, the area is a small area, it's a small state, so they think they can learn about the history of the state rapidly. You know, between a fly and a man, the DNA of a fly and a man is different. Well, the difference is 3 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'll interrupt you there because I don't believe you have understood my question. You haven't understood the importance of my question. All the questions I put are important; otherwise, I remain silent, I don't put questions. So when I do put a question, believe me, it's important. It's a result of something I have thought through. I'm trying to see matters in a clear manner. Things are very complicated. I have the testimony of a witness in front of me. He testified under oath, and he is supposed to tell the truth to the best of his ability. And what is it that this witness claims? He says that he had a lengthy conversation with Siljeg, Siljeg showed him numerous maps, and he showed him something that related to the Croatian Banovina, and this is at the heart of the Prosecution case, in fact. The journalist then adds, while sitting in the place you are now occupying, and he adds this in line 14, he says that this was not HVO policy at all. We don't know why he made such a claim, but this is what he claimed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He continues to say that these policies were policies pursued by its rival, the HOS. So this foreigner, who had contact with Siljeg, listened to Siljeg, who spoke to him perhaps about the Banovina, and this foreigner said that this was not HVO policy, and this is what I'm trying to understand. I'm asking myself, Siljeg, who was he? Did he share the ideas of the HOS or did he just take the maps out to give this journalist a lesson in history, or was Siljeg in favour of a banovina, but that did not necessarily imply that the HVO was also involved in this? The journalist says that the HVO didn't pursue such policies or support such policies, so I'm trying to understand the matter. Have you understood my question more fully now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. The answer is the HVO didn't pursue any policies that supported the Banovina, not at any point in time. It recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on and so forth. Siljeg couldn't represent the policies of the Banovina because he was a commander in the operative zone and he had absolutely nothing to do with this. The HOS [realtime transcript read in error "HVO"] did support policies of an entirely different kind; not only policies that supported a banovina, they wanted a Croatia that reached as far as the Drina River, Your Honours, a Croatia as far as the Drina. I don't know how this was to be done -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I think there has been a significant error in the transcript. Page 37, line 24, the General said the "HOS supported entirely different policies," not "the HVO supported entirely different policies." I think this has to be corrected. General, could you perhaps confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The HOS wanted to pursue the policies enforced in the Second World War, policies of the then independent state of Croatia, which claimed that the Croatian state should extend as far as the Drina River. They said that Muslims were Croats of Islamic faith. In the worst-case scenario, well, Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be a confederation -- or at least Bosnia-Herzegovina should be in Federation with Croatia and reach as far as the Drina, but in these extreme policies the idea was that the Serbs should leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, they should be expelled. Unfortunately, such HOS policies, not of everyone in the HOS - there are many honest fighters who later transferred to the HVO - but unfortunately commanders of the ABiH accepted such policies while it suited them, and this is what was ugly in this entire story.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may paraphrase my client, General Petkovic, could you please put the following question to General Praljak with regard to this transcript that reflects Vulliamy's testimony? If we have a look at line 12, a reference is made to the future Croatian Federation. Line 13, it says that it was a Croatia that extended almost as far as Belgrade. The name of a town is mentioned, but it's not correct. The town is, in fact, Zemun, it should say "Zemun." It's the town of Zemun. And then it says that this is a state that existed in 1941 and that it's a state that was also supported by the HOS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So perhaps General Praljak could tell us which state is, in fact, concerned and whether the description provided by Vulliamy, that it's a Croatian banovina, is that correct, or is it a different state that is concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an objection that the Prosecution would like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I know it doesn't seem that way, but actually this is the Prosecution cross-examination, or at least it was a half hour ago. And, you know, I will say, Mr. President, there is a bit of frustration on my part. I feel as though the level of intervention is increasing. An observation has been made that the questions could be more focused. It's probably a correct observation. I can only say that it's really hard to do this when you're having to do it in fits and starts. And I know -- and, I mean, we're obviously grateful and the Trial Chamber's highly attentive and interested, and these issues about the HVO and the HOS were clearly significant enough, I was going to raise them myself before moving on. But while we're here, if I could respectfully request, perhaps, if I could flag for the Trial Chamber when I've finished a particular document, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. To make a -- we're going to have a break now. Finish with this document. Madam Alaburic, your comments were not absolutely necessary because I saw, myself, that there was lines 14 and 15 and that we need to understand it better. Unfortunately, I have to say that when Vulliamy came, we didn't have all the documents that arrived later, so when he said this, this escaped me, I didn't think it was so interesting, but now, with hindsight, of course it requires further precision. If Vulliamy were here, I would ask him to explain, How could you, as a journalist, make the distinction between the HOS and the HVO, et cetera. But at the time he came, we didn't have all the documents, and that is why we wanted to specify this. It is time for the break. Mr. Stringer will see if he can be here tomorrow morning, and he will tell us later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We'll go into closed session because counsel for Mr. Coric has something to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have lost one of the lenses from my glasses, so I will not be able to see properly. However, as I envisaged that this might happen, I left a reserve pair of spectacles here in a cupboard. So could somebody fetch them for me, that is, my reserve spectacles, because I expected this to happen? But in the meantime, I can manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go and fetch them yourself. Is it nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Defence locker. I keep them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already informed the Case Manager and told him to fetch it for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'll give the floor to Mr. Stringer. He can continue, and he will try and avoid asking you to look at documents until your glasses arrive. So, Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you don't feel comfortable answering my questions until you have your glasses, General, just tell me and I'll stop. I want to come back to this -- the testimony of Mr. Vulliamy that we were talking about before the break. Now -- and I was asking you about the periods of time and the division of labour which made Mr. Siljeg's area of responsibility sort of your top priority, if I could put it that way, during the time that you were the commander of the HVO Main Staff. Is that an acceptable way of putting it, that your priority was the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone, at least during August and September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Because of the operations of the ABiH, this was the priority issue. Their operation started from Bugojno, and it was militarily the most sensitive and most difficult section.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you were in the Prozor area or that operative zone August/September 1993. We know that you were also in that area previously from late October until about the 24th of December, 1993. So is it fair to say, General, that you had -- and I know that you say you didn't work closely with him. Did you have frequent dealings and interactions with Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was there in 1993, yes, we cooperated very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, during 1992, during late October until Christmas of 1992, when you were in Prozor, Tomislavgrad, Gornji Vakuf --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you were in Prozor, did you work out of the headquarters where Colonel Siljeg was located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very, very rarely, because it was just an effort to calm the situation in Rama. After that, I went on to Travnik. Most of the rest of this period I spent between Travnik and Vitez. Then I would go back to Konjic, which -- in view of an operation there which the armija later cancelled, then the operation at Komar, et cetera. Please don't be offended, but your questions are too general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The reference in the transcript here from Mr. Vulliamy, where Colonel Siljeg told him that Prozor was now clean, General, this was, in fact, one of the purposes and results of the HVO operation in Prozor in late October; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect, Mr. Stringer. First, I don't know what Siljeg said to Vulliamy, but I do know what I was doing and what was the position of the political structures of the HVO, because I was in contact with them. For heaven's sake, if they didn't agree with the policy of return and calming down of the situation, they would have sent me away. The HVO in those days, in 20 or 25 days, could have defeated the still weak Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and disarm them, so what you are trying to achieve is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that when Siljeg referred to the drunken celebrations outside as sort of a "boys will be boys" sort of conduct, if, in fact, that was his attitude, it would set a command climate in his operative zone that would not be appropriate and would, in fact, lead to unprofessional conduct on the part of subordinates; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may intervene for the transcript. I didn't hear it. Whether the transcript is incorrect or not, but in the question was when Siljeg spoke about the drunken celebrations. In the document, it's Vulliamy who's talking about it and not Siljeg, so I think we have to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll read the transcript again. Vulliamy says: "He made a reference to the rather drunken celebrations outside as night games, as boys will sort of way."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, General, what Vulliamy is telling us is Siljeg was tolerating drunken behaviour by his subordinates, that he was aware of; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is what Vulliamy says. I cannot comment on this in any other way but to say that I know that Siljeg, nor anyone else in the HVO, tolerated this. There were hundreds of documents, including my own; close all the bars, introduce a curfew. As far as this is concerned, it is true, from the report of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and their representatives that I contacted in Rama, there were drunken soldiers of the HOS who, I repeat, were roasting that lamb. And the report says that Praljak was astonished, he tried to deal with it, they didn't respect him. In the final analysis, I managed to deal with it. That's what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Colonel Siljeg's attitude in respect of this conduct. And if Vulliamy is to be believed, then what we have is a situation where the operative zone commander is tolerating or shows no discomfort with sort of drunken celebration, unprofessional military conduct that is being -- that he's referring to; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to the best of my ability, I don't know what to tell you. Siljeg, in all the contacts we had, did not tolerate these things that Vulliamy is talking about. Now, what Vulliamy says that he heard Siljeg telling him, how can I guess? As commander of the operative zone, Siljeg never tolerated -- neither did he tolerate, nor was this permissible. Throughout the war, I didn't take a single glass of alcohol, not even a glass of wine. And, believe me, I like wine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the reference here on the Banovina, the HVO, and the HOS policy. Now, Vulliamy is a journalist from the United Kingdom, he works for the "Guardian," he's arrived in this area, Prozor area, and in his testimony he tells us about his conversation with Siljeg, and Vulliamy makes reference to the so-called banovina, the Banovina Croatia. Now, the fact is that Vulliamy would only have gotten that word -- those words, "Banovina for Croatia," from Siljeg in the context of such a conversation; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection to the form of the question. I think this is totally improper, and I believe it is time -- high time, I would say, that the Trial Chamber take control over this cross-examination and limit it to its scope and nature. First of all, how can this question be possibly answered? Assuming that Vulliamy is what he claims to be, and might I remind everyone that we -- I tendered testimony by way of Dr. Schindler's book where Vulliamy indicated in an interview that he must take sides in a war, meaning that he's not an objective observer, but how can --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This person, if he is what he is, can certainly read, and this is a historical fact, and anybody can know about this. To now ask this question as if -- this is only through this person individual, that is Siljeg, that someone who is as internationally renowned as Vulliamy could have gotten this information is pure and unadulterated poppycock, and I don't think this is proper cross-examinations, none of this is. Now, the Prosecution put on its case. They had every opportunity, if they wished to, to bring Siljeg into this courtroom and impeach him, and to try to validate what Siljeg has told, supposedly, to Vulliamy through this particular witness is utterly improper. I have never seen any of this sort of cross-examination in a courtroom, and I don't think that as relaxed as we are in this particular system, that this sort of cross-examination should be tolerated. It has no value whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. The general's challenged the testimony of Ed Vulliamy. I'm asking him questions about Siljeg and the conversation. I'm putting the Prosecution case to the witness. The witness is free to disregard and to disagree with me, as he has on numerous occasions. Now, there is questions -- there is obviously interest on the part of the Trial Chamber about this part of the conversation, and I think I'm entitled to put the cross-examination case on it to the witness. If he disagrees with me, that's fine, but I don't know that this is terribly different than anything that's been happening in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The problem, Your Honour, is that General Praljak was not present. We don't even know how this conversation took place. And might I remind everyone in this courtroom, because I certainly haven't forgotten it, that when Mr. Vulliamy was here we had very tight dead-lines as far as being able to cross-examine the gentleman. And so now to somehow try to bolster Vulliamy's testimony through this witness, I don't see how you can possibly place any weight on it. You can accept Vulliamy's testimony as you wish, but to suggest that somehow General Praljak can opine as to what was in Siljeg's mind when, supposedly, he made these comments, which are counter-intuitive, by the general's remarks thus far, I don't see how it benefits the Trial Chamber. We are not getting anywhere. What I am seeing, however, is the abuse of allowing either side an enormous amount of time for cross-examination, which is why we're spending two or three hours to try to make one point that, in the end of the day, is rather mindless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber, after deliberation, would like to learn from Mr. Stringer the precise questions that he wishes to put to General Praljak concerning the words of Mr. Vulliamy and what he told us when he was testifying. Before the Chamber being able to say anything, we would like to know the area of the questions that you're going to put, because we are a bit in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question would be this, Mr. President, whether the witness agrees with me that when Siljeg spoke of the banovina, he was, in fact, telling Vulliamy what precisely was HVO policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, how do we know that he actually spoke? Do we have a tape of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Because I think that this is a question which really calls for speculation. It calls for the witness to say what he thinks that Mr. Siljeg thought, and I do not think that it is proper to ask that kind of question. I hope you also agree, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel has responded, so, Mr. Stringer, please move on. If you wish to stay on this subject, approach it differently, because it is very difficult, as my colleague has said, talking about a witness who was not present during a conversation, to enter into the thoughts of the two participants at that meeting. That is rather complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's best to move on to something else. I, personally, when I asked a question about what Mr. Vulliamy might have said, and I noted that Vulliamy said that that was not the policy of the HVO, but rather of the HOS. That is as far as I went. I didn't go into the thoughts of either of the two. So please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P00721, and it is a report of the SIS, Municipal Staff, Prozor, 8th of November, 1992. There are initials that appear at the bottom of it. One of those is "LM." General, we've talked -- you've talked a fair amount or at various times in your testimony you've spoken about reports -- SIS reports of Luka Markesic. Do you agree with me that possible or, indeed, even likely that he's the "LM" that's referred to here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible and highly probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, he's reporting on the situation in the town following the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH, and he says that: "A large number of the civilian population fled. Due to extensive material damage, the town has been largely deserted. However, over the past couple of days, the situation has begun to normalise and people started to return to their homes and repair the damaged facilities." And I'm going to skip the next paragraph, and he says: "Large-scale thefts of both private and community properties have taken place, including goods, vehicles, and even arms." And then he says: "The military police have done nothing in that respect, neither have it issued receipts on seised items, which enabled a certain number of military policemen to take possession of the seised items and arms." Now, General, just a few questions there on these last two paragraphs. Based on what you saw and observed during your time in Prozor here, do you agree with this statement that there were, in fact, large-scale thefts of both private and community properties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that I have already said was that I confirmed that there were thefts, and that is true. The only problem is when we talk about the amounts or the quantity, unfortunately, nobody indicates a number. Now, what Luka Markesic means when he says "large-scale," I don't know. Is 10 or 50 for him "large-scale"? Unfortunately, reports are not precise enough determining the quantity or the numbers of what is being reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then when he says in the next paragraph that: "The military police have done nothing in that respect ...," do you agree with that statement as well, that the military police, in fact, did nothing to prevent the large-scale thefts that he referred to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. SIS and the military police should have collaborated. I know with certainty, because I spoke about it, and that is that Valentin Coric did issue an order, and I saw it here, that the cars should be collected. To what extent they succeeded, I don't know, because after the release of prisoners and after the population returned, I left to go to Travnik because Central Bosnia was in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then he says that the Command is working on appointing a new military police commander, and then he continues -- or the reports continues and it says: "The conflict was followed by introduction of curfew, which is not adhered to in most of the cases and, as a result, drunk armed individuals, members of our units, frequently fire their weapons. They even steal and burn private facilities, in spite of the fact that the conflict is over and that the situation is calming down." Now, General, is that, indeed, the situation that you observed when you were in Prozor, following the conflict there, when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there were such problems, Mr. Stringer. There's no doubt about it. But this person's duty is to say -- this is the Security Service. He should say, Such and such a soldier, at such and such a time, in such and such a place, did such and such a thing, and then, according to my information, these people torched this building. So this is a general story, and then when you ask someone, Who are we going to arrest and who are we going to prosecute, then this paper means nothing at all. And then he also says that 90 per cent of those who had done what they did had already fled the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, he continues on to say: "A great number of those who are responsible for the conflict, about 90 per cent of them, are at large and out of our municipality, while those less responsible either do not feel responsible at all or they report to the military police themselves, and some of them are forcefully brought in and disarmed by the military police. We have to admit that the military police are more or less powerless when it comes to seizing and returning the taken property, and therefore we deem that the only solution is engaging a military police unit from elsewhere." Now, General, the fact is that a big part of the problem in Prozor was the military police, itself; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the man who, according to establishment, should have authority over. The military police has written that. Now, who is he writing to? The military police, according to establishment, should have been a part of the SIS, S-I-S. I don't know. I know that there were problems. I know how dealt with them. Of course, I couldn't run from one bar to another, nor did I have such authority, nor is it physically possible. I calmed the situation down in that area to the best of my ability with the assistance of many people, Siljeg and others, not on my own. Not that there were problems; there were, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we're going to be talking sometime soon, maybe tomorrow, about Gornji Vakuf and the events that happened there in January of 1993. Based on the experience in Prozor, General, would you agree with me that you and any HVO commander, who is commanding HVO units at Gornji Vakuf in January, should have been well aware of the possibility that HVO units and soldiers would get involved in criminal activities as part of or following military operations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I could answer that. Naturally, every civilian in every town, in any place, can be involved in some sort of a crime. I don't know how I could answer such a conditional question. Anyone can become a criminal at any point in time. No one is immune to this. No one can claim for certain that such a thing might never occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And based on the events in Prozor, where the HVO committed a number of crimes, thefts, looting, at the very least, that we've been talking about, you and Siljeg were on notice that, in fact, the same sorts of crimes were likely to occur when military operations were conducted in Gornji Vakuf; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, the HVO never committed any crimes. Individuals commit crimes. For the HVO to commit crimes, it would have been necessary to issue orders -- for orders to have been issued, for this to have been authorised or suggested, but this was never done, from Mate Boban to Petkovic to myself and so on. Individuals can do such things. They're held to account. There are investigations, charges, convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You knew that a significant number of HVO individuals committed crimes in Prozor; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A significant number of HVO individuals didn't commit crimes. I didn't know about that, I didn't know which individuals were concerned, which municipalities they had came from, where they came from, because 90 per cent of them, according to the report, fled, so it's certain that in that area there were a certain number of criminals who were present. This wasn't written on their foreheads, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you knew and Colonel Siljeg knew, Brigadier Petkovic knew, that it would be necessary to closely monitor and to implement measures to prevent similar crimes from taking place in Gornji Vakuf; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have the assumption that crimes were perpetrated in Gornji Vakuf. I'm not aware of that. The first thing is correct. In each and every place, we referred to continual training, to rules, to duties, preparation for operations. Whenever there were preparations for operations, we spoke about military conduct. Whatever a commander could do, did it in the HVO. If there were any violations, this would be noted after an investigation and the procedure would be followed such as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A technical question, General Praljak. I have noticed that this report was drafted -- when it was drafted, there were two copies. It's the last sentence in the document, so there are two copies. We don't know where the copies were sent to. Where was the document found, the one we have in B/C/S? We can see the stamp from the archives, but where was it found? So I have a series of questions there. Nevertheless, in your opinion, in technical terms, the SIS report is usually addressed to whom, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was -- what was it called? There was part of the SIS for the operative zone. I don't know whether it was in Tomislavgrad or Livno. And there's a SIS administration that sends the second document. I think those two copies were sent to the person responsible. I don't know. Stojic, don't intervene. I'm talking about what is possible. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] May I say something? Where does it say that it went somewhere, that it was sent somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say "I think." I'm not asking you about what you think. Usually, in military terms, an SIS report should be addressed to whom, exactly? To whom is such a report sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't express any opinions, I won't say what I think, so in that case I don't know. The SIS wasn't part of the Main Staff, so you should bring someone from the SIS here to answer the question so that I don't have to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can't answer the question. That's sufficient for me. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to draw your attention to what you already noticed in the case of a document. You asked whether the document was a military one.
