I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that in the heading of this document it says the "Stozer Municipal Staff," and within that staff, the SIS, within that framework, the SIS. So when we have a look at all the SIS reports, I believe it's very difficult to speculate, and I don't think it would be a good thing to speculate as to whom these documents were addressed to, because as part of the Municipal Staff there were a number of addressees to whom this report could have been sent. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, although, I was asked to express my opinion, but it could be completely false -- completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, this is just a hypothesis, but let's take the following hypothesis: This SIS report is sent to the Defence Department, but I have no proof for this, of course. Given such a hypothesis, I put the following question to myself with regard to criminal enterprise, of which Mr. Stojic and others are a part: If there is a criminal enterprise that includes the whole series of individuals, would the department of the person who is part of the criminal enterprise draft a report to say, This is what is happening? I'm trying to find a logic behind all of this, because I have already raised this issue. As far as I can remember, there was a military document that said that there were cases of people being rounded up in Mostar, and so on and so forth, so I already raised the issue. I'm raising it once more now, and I'm saying that if this report is sent to the Department of Defence - we don't know whether that is the case or not, I have no evidence - but in that case would the subordinate inform the superior and say, Look, this is what has been happening? I'm trying to be logical here. So you, without speculating, in purely logical terms, would you say that something of this kind would be done, but as there's a Department X, for example -- well, Ms. Nozica said, It could be the Municipal Staff, please pay attention to this. Everything is possible, but in logical terms, if you have a military administrative structure, would the subordinate inform his superior of what was being done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. If this hypothesis is accepted, you could call Mr. Markesic, you could call his superior, or whoever else may have been concerned. This wouldn't have been done. It wouldn't be logical, for example, for me to allow a TV team to go to a prison to show what I had done as a criminal. That would be crazy. One would conceal that. If anyone had wanted to do anything, not even a madman would have written down, Look, we have such and such an intention, and, urbi et orbi, he would say what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this report, and we don't know to whom it is addressed because there's no information about that, and as a result a criminal judge has to proceed by creating a number of hypotheses, but is this report drafted for the military prosecutor? If that is the case, the military prosecutor has to react. Is it for the civilian prosecutor? If so, the civilian prosecutor has to react to it. If the report is intended for the commander of the Prozor-Rama Brigade - well, then there's this matter of disarmed individuals - well, should the brigade commander then have to react or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A brigade commander can't react, because it's not his job. Judge Antonetti, I know Luka Markesic fairly well. He's a very honest, good man, in a certain way. But when you have such information, information that he provided to me up there, well, my question to Markesic was, Give me a name, a first and last name. Who, where, when? Of what use is it to relay information that you obtain someone? You can take action if you have a first and last name. Who stole things, who opened fire, and so on and so forth. There were difficulties, naturally, when it comes to bringing people in. This is all noted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, the person who received this report, shouldn't he have asked for an additional report in order to have the perpetrators identified, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given this is an organisation that was separate from what I was involved in in 1993, well, I would refrain from answering a question by speculating as to what should have been done, that probably should have been done. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I apologise. I didn't want to intervene, but -- and I apologise to my colleague, but I would like to draw your attention to a paragraph in this document which is a partial answer that doesn't involve speculation, a partial answer to a series of your questions, because here it says many of those guilty for this conflict, about 90 per cent of them have fled, they have left our municipality, whereas those who are less guilty or not considered to be guilty have handed themselves in, to a large extent, to the military police. A smaller number of them have been brought in by force and disarmed by the military police. Without speculating in any way, I can draw the conclusion from this paragraph that this does not concern unidentified individuals. Someone, the SIS or the commander of the brigade, of the military police, identified these individuals and took action against them. So we know that there are 90 per cent who have fled, and those they have access to are the subject of investigations, of actions. So this is information on the event and on action taken, if you read through the entire document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Praljak, Ms. Nozica is perfectly right, and I did notice that 10 per cent of them had been identified because they had been disarmed. But my question concerns the 90 per cent who are elsewhere. The person who drafted the report said that this wasn't within his remit, so in that case, with regard to those who are elsewhere, the 90 per cent who hadn't been identified, who should have been responsible for dealing with this matter, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if they were soldiers, then the SIS has to investigate the matter. If they were civilians or weren't part of the military structure, for example, if it was the HOS, in that case the civilian police would have been responsible for the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We won't go any further because we've spent a lot of time on the subject, but my colleague has a question or some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: One rather brief question. Mr. Praljak, on page 58, lines 6 to 9, you have said that Mr. Markesic was an honest, good man, and then you say: "My question to Markesic was, Give me a name, a first and a last name, who were they, who, where, when." Now, this could give the idea that you have actually seen this report, the one that we do not know to whom it was sent. Did you see a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no, Judge Trechsel. When I was up there, when I noticed this breakdown of order, I spoke to him. But as far as I know, he only had one other man in that department with him, and then on one or two occasions he came to see me with similar information, and I said, Well, look -- the rest you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought this should be clarified. Please, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is 3D00424. This is one of your documents. You've talked about it already in your direct examination. This is a document issued jointly by yourself and Valentin Coric on ordering that the cars taken away from the people at Prozor be returned to them. Just a couple of questions about this. The order, General, in the heading or the letterhead part is dated the 14th of November, 1992, but then there are notations to the left of Mr. Coric's signature, which are above your signature, which indicate that the order's being directed to Colonel Siljeg and that the dead-line for implementation of the order is 2000 hours on the 19th of December, 1992. So there is more than a month between the date of the order and the date of its implementation, and I was just wondering if you could shed some light on that for us. Was it your intention to allow for about five weeks for the implementation of this order to take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, sir. This order obviously consists of two parts. This is an order to the Military Police Administration, signed by Mr. Coric, or someone signed on his behalf. He's put it in the present tense. He says the vehicles that were confiscated from those who had confiscated them, those vehicles are located in a certain place, they have to be given to Ante Alilovic, who will ensure that the vehicles are returned to their owners. This order has to be implemented by the 17th of November, so from the -- between the 14th and 17th of November, up until 1200 hours, and this is to be done by Zdenko Andabak. But the order to Siljeg, as to what that concerns, I have no idea, but it's not the same thing. Something was sent to him, and he had to take action, and I signed all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, did you -- assuming that Mr. Coric signed this order on the 14th of November, 1992, did you also sign it on the 14th of November?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you didn't add your signature later on or about sometime in December, directing it specific to Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think we drafted this together. I didn't add anything to the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this order does not contain any reference to investigation or punishing people responsible for taking all the vehicles. General, did you, yourself, issue any orders requiring investigation or prosecution of individuals responsible for taking all the cars that are the subject of this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I didn't. I co-signed this order, I gave it a certain weight. I didn't have the right to issue orders to what you are saying. I made requests. The order on returning doesn't also have to contain information on action to be taken against those who are guilty. This is the responsibility of the military police, and then punishment is meted out on the basis of the person who has been captured. Here, this has to do with returning -- this order has to do with returning the cars by the 17th of November, the cars that were confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, it says here the cars were located at the stations of the 2nd Military Police Battalion and that they have to be transported and handed over to this person in Ljubuski. General, do you know where the cars were located on or about the 14th of November, when this order was issued? Where's the location of the 2nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. It says what it says here. Apart from very normal conversations about the issue -- about the issue that they should be returned, and this was Coric's desire as well, and what was seised was seised, apart from that...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So assuming that all of these vehicles went from Prozor, where the owners lived, and ultimately ended up in Ljubuski, as referenced in this order, you don't know how they would have gotten from Prozor to Ljubuski or down into the Ljubuski area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But as people were captured, well, then this was obviously taken to two places. Zdenko Andabak was to -- well, I think the 2nd Battalion was in Livno or Tomislavgrad, so the vehicles have to be gathered and someone had to process them. And then once they had been gathered, they would be transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It just seems to me it would have been quite a logistical effort to transport all these cars down to Ljubuski, and I'm wondering whether you have any information about that aspect of this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, no one transported them to Ljubuski. As the car would be seised, you had to take the car to a place that was protected, and naturally that was a place where the military police had some sort of parking space which they could supervise. And once they had gathered them, they'd be transported to their owners. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit, unless there are questions on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, General Praljak, I've been listening to you and I have been wondering about the following. You will tell me whether this is realistic or not. We know that there are a certain number of vehicles that were "confiscated," in inverted commas. In the previous document, we saw that 10 per cent of the perpetrators were identified, so one might think that the police were doing their work. The police gathered the vehicles, and they were all gathered in Ljubuski. That took a certain amount of time. On the 14th of November, Mr. Coric issues an order according to which these vehicles are to be returned by the 17th of November, by 1200 hours on the 17th of November. So this is an order on returning the vehicles. And then you, on the 18th of December, perhaps on the 17th, but on the 18th, and you'll see why, you discover the problem, because perhaps you heard about the fact that some vehicles weren't returned. At that point in time, you write on the document that you had a little note stating that by the 19th of December, at 2000 hours, the order that apparently hasn't been implemented should be implemented. It's on the 18th of December that you come to this realisation. But have a look at the document. You can see that there's a fax. It says the 18th of December, noon, 1200 hours. Perhaps one should have identified this number, 38, 58, et cetera. You discover there's still a problem, and you do what is necessary, and you say, Return them. And the following day -- noon of the following day is the dead-line, because otherwise how could one explain the following? You sign on the 14th of November, and you give them five weeks to return vehicles that were already -- or that had already been gathered. So what I am saying: Would you say that this is possible, impossible? I don't know. What would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]I don't know either, Your Honour. However much I try, I can't remember all the details. I know our position was that vehicles should be returned, but as to what this means, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I think a different reading of the document is possible. I read it slightly differently. I think that the dead-line -- this order must be implemented by 1200 hours on 17 November, refers to the order to transfer the cars to the deputy chief of the General and Traffic Military Police, Ante Alilovic. This transfer must occur before the 17th, and this something which can easily be done because you know where you're going. Whereas, I can imagine that it is not so easy, even if you have the car, to find all the owners and get them to come and pick up their cars, and that would explain that the second phase, namely, the first [indiscernible] is a car from one place within the HVO to another place within the HVO, the second phase is from the HVO to owner, and that second phase, I could imagine, was not so easily performed as the first phase, and therefore a longer period was provided for the implementation. How does that appear to you as a hypothesis, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is, once again, that the number of events and problems, from the moment I arrived until Christmas, the defence of Travnik, meetings, there were so many events that I can accept this, and I can't say more than that the vehicles had to be returned. And I think that the government even made a decision to financially compensate the owners, but Mr. Prlic could tell you more about that than me. I simply can't claim with any certainty what was really happened [as interpreted]. Maybe there was a problem with returning those vehicles to their owners, and then I'm addressing myself to Siljeg. I simply can't say with certainty, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, there is a more important subject than the question of vehicles, and which appears in the document. You know that the Prosecutor's case is that you were the commander prior to the 27th of July. On the 19th of December, you issue this order, you write a comment, but I note that there is a stamp with number "1" on it. Look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, like me, that stamps are used under very precise conditions. It's not anyone that is entitled to use a stamp, et cetera. So the person who put the stamp on the document, after your signature, it could be you, a secretary, or anyone, but anyone who has stamped the document "Praljak number 1," he must think that you have the authority given by this stamp. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. It is for the first time here in court that I heard that stamps have a number that has any importance. Let me say, for the hundredth time, I was not the commander, I was the assistant. I didn't pay any attention to stamps at all, nor did I know who was stamping what. The -- 99.9 per cent of my energy, my thoughts, my intelligence was focused on what I have said; to calm the situation down, to reconcile people, to help in establishing joint command, to defend Travnik. Even there I assumed a role that I shouldn't have had. When no one else is reacting and the whole valley is going to fall, I didn't have the authority of a commander, but I did command in Travnik. So what else could I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'm going to stop you there because you have given a long answer. You say that it was for the first time in this Tribunal that you discovered the importance and the existence of stamps. That's what you are saying. You are saying this under oath, so I may believe you and I may also have my doubts. But this means that the HVO commander did not know that stamps had a certain significance. And you are telling us that only when you got here did you realise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, Your Honours. I am saying it under oath, that I discovered the importance of these numbers only when I got here to -- in the Tribunal. That's how it was, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. According to my recollection, documents from the JNA, and this must apply also to the ABiH and the HVO - they had the same rules - stamps have numbers. And there aren't 36 stamps, so a stamp that was put, where was it physically? When you signed, in which office did you sign this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There's no point in pursuing my question any further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably where General Petkovic was. I can't remember just now, but if the stamp was in the Main Staff, then I must have done it in the Main Staff, in Petkovic's office or -- I don't know, I can't remember. I repeat, under oath, stamps did not mean anything to me. Whether that is wrong or not, that is how it was. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I should like to return briefly to the issue prior to this one with the stamps. Though the stamp is illegible, perhaps it would be useful, as this is a document of the 3D Defence, that we look at the original document, and we see that there is certain commas, and at the top it says "aorist," the past perfect tense. So it would be useful to ask the general whether he knows who put these markings on the document and what does this word in the upper right-hand corner mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I noticed that "aorist" was indicated on the text, and I was wondering what this is. Perhaps you can tell us. How would you interpret this, "aorist" and then a line, what does all this mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "aorist," which is a tense which, in the Croatian language, is the past perfect text. So we can again engage in guess-work and say this was Siljeg or someone else. Anyway, he said "aorist," which would mean, according to the Croatian language, what is being required by this order has already been carried out. It's a verb, an action. "Aorist" is a verb tense which indicates that the action was completed in the past, so it's the past perfect. The order has been fulfilled, that is what this person wants to indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Stringer, we took some time, but it was necessary to fully exhaust this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document is P01327, 1327, and this one is dated the 27th of January. It's addressed to the military police from the brigade commander, Simun Zutic. And, General, the first question is this, because we looked earlier at an order or a document of the brigade commander of the Rama Brigade, and that was Mr. Franjo --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Franjic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Franjo Franjic; Ilija Franjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, does this -- does this indicate now that the Rama Brigade has a different commander and his name is Zutic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may. I seem to recall that in the document where Mr. Franjic signed, it was indicated "for the commander, Franjic." Maybe we could -- if you recall the number, we could look at it. It is document 00 -- P00662.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, 662.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you have -- I read the English, handwritten, "for brigade commander," which would indicate that Ilija Franjic is not the brigade commander, because he is the one who writes. In the original, it is "Za," in handwriting before the name, "Za Zapovjednik Brigade."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, the brigade commander is Ilija Franjic, but as he was not there to sign the document, it was signed by Zutic on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That is not excluded. I can take it that the signature is Zutic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just ask it this way, General. Perhaps you can just tell us. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: January 27, 1993, do you know who is the brigade commander of the Rama Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't like to guess. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The earlier document, which was from October of 1992, the Ilija Franjic document --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, either. I can't say with any certainty. All this is guess-work. I don't feel well when I am guessing. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In any event, in this report, and now we're back to P01327, in this report to the military police, the author of this is informing the members of the military police at the check-points in the Prozor municipality of the following: 1. No Muslims are allowed to go through the area of this municipality. 2. Check buses going through the area of our municipality --" MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend, but maybe an error in the translation or maybe he misspoke, but on page 70, line 16 and 17, the question speaks about a report, and from the document we see that it is not a report, but an order. And I think the distinction is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it's an order, clearly, not a report, and the order is that, as is indicated here: "No Muslims are allowed to go through the municipality." Secondly, that buses should be checked, and that Muslims on the buses should be removed, and that the goods and cargo that Muslims try to take through the area of Prozor should be confiscated. And then the order is that this takes effect immediately and all of the military police check-points should be informed of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, first question: Would you agree with me that this is an illegal order, in that it makes no distinction between Muslim civilians, combatants, military reasons why people would be treated in this way versus --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of this order, which was issued in the couple of weeks or so after the events in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I take it from what you've said, General, then, that you would not approve of such an order or approve of a practice or the practices that are being required in this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the military police in Prozor carried out this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, because on the 23rd of January, I left the area. I could have even been there without knowing everything that was going on. It doesn't mean that if you're in a certain area, you know everything that someone might do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further on that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted briefly to draw attention to something. I don't know whether there were any errors in the transcript; I think not. But when I read through twice, what I see, there was a certain misunderstanding. And as these are your questions, Your Honour, perhaps it would be best if you could clarify this. On page 66, line 9, there is the question, and then line 17 the answer, and it's almost identical; that is, repeated on page 67, line 2, when your question starts, and line 10, Praljak's answer. It's about the conversation about the stamp. You're asking Praljak about the stamps, and Mr. Praljak obviously is answering about the number appearing within that stamp, so as if you were not on the same frequency, so it emerges that Praljak was not aware of the significance of stamps. What he really was saying is, I never realised that the numbers within the stamp are of significance. Perhaps you could clarify this, because in this way it will be quite unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, let us specify. When an officer signs a document, there is a stamp, and in ex-Yugoslavia these stamps carried numbers, and the numbers corresponded to position, number 1 being the highest, 2 below that, et cetera. When you answered my questions, your reply included the stamp and the number or exclusively the number within the stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give me a minute, please. I never took a stamp and stamped a document with it. In the former Yugoslavia, there were millions of stamps on hundreds of papers, on documents. This was something I didn't like. I always admired the Americans, who would sign a diploma and there would never be a stamp, whereas in our country there were millions of stamps and the papers meant nothing. In view of this, and the fact that I had a different job, I knew nothing about stamps or the numbers on the stamps. It was the first time, at this Tribunal, that I realised that a number on the stamp meant something. So I would sign a document, and somebody would stamp it and forward it. Those were my understandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the document which is on the screen, in this document one can again give it two readings, which complicates our task. I'm trying to analyse this document, and the request is that those controlling check-points should verify whether the Muslims have any goods on them, and to confiscate them, and to remove them if they are in the vehicles. That is one understanding. However, what is not clear in the document is whether these are vehicles which are entering the zone or which are leaving the municipality, because the two are quite different. If the order applies to vehicles which are leaving the municipality, one could read into that that the Muslims are being prevented from leaving the municipality, and, due to that, this could have a certain impact on the enterprise, that is, the wish to have the Muslims leave. The situation is different if the Muslims are coming from outside and who wish to enter the municipality. Why are they being prevented, for what reason? Is it because they are bringing aid to those who are already in the municipality, or are they going to reinforce the number of Muslims in the municipality? I don't know. So this document, for a Judge who reads it, poses a number of problems; hence my question. You have condemned this document, you have already said that, but according to you, who has full control of the language, what was the purpose of this document; to prevent the Muslims from entering, to make them leave? What was the actual aim of this document, if there was an objective behind it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this document, I cannot give this document a single interpretation. It is a semi-literate document which one cannot interpret simply and clearly; at least I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, perhaps it's time for the break. I see it's already 20 to 6.00. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume. You have until 10 to 7.00, because we shouldn't forget that Counsel Kovacic needs a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P02526, 2526. Now, we're still in Prozor municipality, but we're moving forward in time. This is an order from General Petkovic to the Ljubuski Brigade regarding sending of units to Prozor, and he's saying due to the exceptionally complex situation around Bugojno and the threat to Vakuf and Prozor, he orders that company-strength forces are immediately to be prepared and sent to Prozor. The company commander is to report to General Slobodan Praljak. General, this is from May of 1993, the 26th of May, so this is after the conflict between ABiH and HVO forces in Mostar that broke out on the 9th/10th of May. General, is it correct, as is indicated or as suggested here, that at this time you were in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, at the time I was briefly in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where, precisely -- when you say you were in Prozor, just -- again just to be clear -- well, tell me first, what were you doing in Prozor or what was the purpose for your being there at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the assistant for General Petkovic that was ordered -- I issued an order about this, as a volunteer. Well, after the attack of the ABiH on the 9th of May in Mostar, after the situation had been calmed down in Mostar, well, similarly it was necessary to calm the situation down on the Bugojno-Uskoplje-Gornji Vakuf axis, and to this effect there were very -- there was very clear information about the fact that the ABiH had already begun to prepare for what was subsequently to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you say you were --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend Mr. Stringer. Could we perhaps correct something in the transcript? It might be important. At line 16 of the page we are now on, it says that the general -- it says that General Praljak said, "I issued an order about this." General Praljak said that he was assisting General Petkovic and that General Petkovic issued an order. I just wanted to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic issued orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you say you were briefly in Prozor at this time. Can you tell us approximately how much time you spent in Prozor during this period, 26th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- couldn't say so, but I wasn't there for long, because after the situation stabilised in Mostar and in that area, after that I returned to Zagreb. As for the date, well, give or take a day, it was a very short period, but no matter how much I would like to, I can't give you precise dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the fact that these units are going to be sent from Ljubuski and are to report to you, General, suggests that even though you didn't have a formal position in the HVO at this time, you did exercise command authority over HVO units. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not command authority, but a certain amount of authority when it comes to assistance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it's like the prisoners we spoke about earlier who were at that place in Prozor, the primary school at Ripci. By virtue of your experience and your attributes, you had authority, and the soldiers -- the HVO soldiers there did what you told them to do. But the same situation then applies in respect of these soldiers, then, coming from Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that they did what I said. The commander of the company would contact me. The men who came from Ljubuski, and I was on good terms with them from the beginning because we had been in combat in 1992 together, I knew them very well. They had to be persuaded about the necessity of leaving or abandoning the territorial war. The necessity of assisting Siljeg. It was assistance, and it wasn't as you described it. It was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you had fought with these soldiers or these units previously, and it was thought that you could exercise some influence and authority over them; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now if General Petkovic is telling them to report to you, then from their point of view, what that means, in military terms, is that you're going to be their commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was to assist with their reception, with explaining to them the reasons for their arrival there, why they had left their municipalities, with regard to assisting Siljeg, to incorporate them in the command structure. It was a matter of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that after reporting to you, they were -- they became part of the operative zone command structure under Colonel Siljeg; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. General, the next exhibit is P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Prosecution has just put a question to you that you answered in negative terms. The Prosecution would like to know whether this document made you the commander of the units that were sent from Ljubuski to go to the Prozor area and the Vakuf area, given the situation that prevailed. You said, No. When we have a look at the order, and I'll put the questions that come to me - I'm quite open about this, I have nothing to hide - the first legal question I have is as follows: In the chain of command, did Mr. Petkovic have the right to directly appoint the superiors of the Ljubuski Brigade? That's my first question. The second question: The order of control, command, communication, the three Cs, this order seems to apply to this because -- applies to this order, because under 3, under item 3, General Petkovic is requesting a report, and if you are taking command, you have to be asked to provide a report, but this is for the Ljubuski Brigade in this case? That's a question that also occurred to me. General Praljak, this order makes you someone who will contribute to the unit or does it integrate you within the chain of command? Does it make you the superior commander of the units sent to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. No, Judge Antonetti. That's my answer to the first question. General Petkovic didn't have the authority to appoint brigade commanders. That was Mate Boban's authority. He could have asked for a replacement, he could have suggested certain appointments, but as far as I know, and I know this in my case, Mate Boban would appoint brigade commanders and relieve them of their duties. Secondly, the Ljubuski Brigade, in item 3 -- under item 3, was to inform him of when they had sent men in and also whether the men had arrived in the area. The Ljubuski Brigade, that's what it says under item 3. There was a significant problem in the HVO, when it came to sending units, as you're well aware, outside of the municipality or the vicinity of the municipality. My relationship with the brigade -- the Ljubuski Brigade commander, Tomic, was taken advantage here. At the very beginning of the war or, in fact, when I arrived in 1992, I met this young man. This brigade was involved in the defence of Capljina, Stolac, et cetera, to a large extent, and I had to incorporate this brigade in the chain of command of Mr. Siljeg. It was a matter of assistance. I was assisting. I had a certain amount of authority. I had the force of persuasion, to a certain extent. But as for the chain of command, as for my ability to issue orders, no, I didn't have such authority, although sometimes I violated this rule. If there was no other way, I'd write something down, and if it worked, it worked; in Travnik, for example, and so on. This wasn't really official, but it was a matter of urgency to avoid a terrible situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would be interested simply to know, factually, and specifically, "concretno," what you did; I went here and told them to do this, and so forth. Would you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I received them, I gave them the political speech. I said that we were under threat, that they had to leave their municipality, that they had to reinforce the lines up there. I said that the ABiH might take action, and I placed them in the chain of command that was Siljeg's or, rather, they were part of the sector that they were to be in. With your leave, Judge Trechsel, Colonel Blaskic, in Travnik, issued, for example, a certain order. The director of a factory that had to produce ammunition wouldn't abide by the order, wouldn't implement the order. General Blaskic didn't know how to implement the order. In that case, since everything was going to fall, I used my force, the fact that I'm corpulent, that I have certain knowledge, that I'm a man of the theatre, and I took things into my own hands. As you saw, that was the case when I had to deal with returning units to their positions. I used my verbal skills. When there was no other way out of the situation, I would do such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You have started being pretty specific, and then you have switched off to general and other incidents and so forth. The last thing we know is you integrated these newly-arrived troops into the -- I think it was the Rama Brigade, probably. Did you divide them up, did you take them to the front, did you take them to a commander and give them over to the commander of the brigade? Afterwards, what did you do? This is the kind of information I would be interested in hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not the Rama Brigade, it's the Ljubuski Brigade, and that's why this was necessary, because it was 100 kilometres from Rama. That's why it was necessary for me to explain to them the purpose of their arrival there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me. The order says: "Send them immediately to Prozor." Prozor, I thought, was an area which was not under control of the Ljubuski Brigade but of the Rama Brigade, but maybe I get this wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, the area of Rama, but they didn't go to Rama but in the direction of Gornji Vakuf. And Siljeg was in command of this, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So did you take them to Siljeg or to a sub-commander of Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, I didn't take them there. They arrived there. They were provided with accommodation. I gave them explanations, and then they received orders from Siljeg as to where they were to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And was that the end of your contribution? You received them, you gave a speech, and then they were left to Siljeg, and you went away, that was the end of your mission? If not, what else did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. I was helping Siljeg. I was helping Siljeg. I spoke to the men. I spoke to them. Much could be achieved through speaking to them. It wasn't necessary to always use orders. They could think of a hundred reasons not to leave Ljubuski, and General Petkovic at the time couldn't do anything that a normal army would do in order to go up there. And you have seen this in the documents. Someone can quite simply leave the territory and not suffer any consequences. You don't know what to do to them. You don't have any other troops. I'm trying to answer to the best of my ability by just providing you with factual answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they had left Ljubuski, because they were now in Gornji Vakuf. So they had already left Ljubuski. So the question whether they liked to do that. And you say, I assisted Colonel Siljeg, I talked to them. I find that it is not clear to me. I cannot imagine how this actually happened. Did you go around and talk to these people individually, or did you assemble sub-groups, or -- I mean, to assist someone is not a very precise description of activity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If at the time, after what had happened in Mostar, General Petkovic hadn't written down that they should report to Praljak, I'm not sure that they would have gone there, because they respected me. It says here, Go up there, General Praljak will receive you, and I'm claiming that that was perhaps the only real reason for which they actually set off on this trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, could I draw your attention to item 4 of the order with regard to this subject? It might assist us in understanding this situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Judge Trechsel, in which order would a commander write -- try and understand this, Prozor and Vakuf under threat? It says, Please try and understand what is at stake. Which army and which state would write something like this? It says, Go and report to General Praljak. This is how the HVO functioned to a large extent. Try and understand. Who, in the American or French Army, would write down, Please, such and such a company should go down there, they are under threat, so if possible, please go there? That's what I'm trying to explain to you. He's pleading. He's trying to make them feel they should go. It's not a military order, if you can understand what I am trying to say. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I see that I do not really get an answer to my question, which is quite specific. I had noted number 4. It was absolutely not necessary to draw our attention to it, Ms. Alaburic. And it is -- it strikes me as a highly unprofessional military order, I must say. You are right, this is not a normal military order, but it seems to me -- I mean, the technique of giving orders seems not to have been very developed in the HVO, which is fully in agreement with much that you have told us. So this is -- this is just evidenced here again. But I think I will not insist, and let Mr. Stringer continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. General Praljak, just a minute. General Praljak, I don't want to linger on this issue, but when you provide an answer and we have a document, I try to regard this in the context of all the evidence that we have seen to date. As a result, I have to perform a sort of intellectual gymnastics so that I have all the information at my disposal. As a result, I'm totally exhausted at the end of each and every hearing. The order that we have before us, I link it to what you have told us, but not only you; others have said the same thing. You said that the military component of the HVO was, in fact -- well, they were, in fact, municipal brigades. They were located in municipalities. And you said that the soldiers, they didn't want to leave their municipalities and they didn't want to go and fight elsewhere. Fine, this stuck in my memory. And here we see that Prozor and Vakuf were in danger. That's under item 4. General Petkovic, who realised the nature of the situation, wanted to send reinforcements to the area, but apparently he hadn't had the Ljubuski Brigade at your disposal. And you said a minute ago that Ljubuski was a hundred kilometres away. And as a result, according to everything you have already said, the men from Ljubuski hesitated to go to Prozor, and this explains the fact that -- or could explain the fact that under item 2 you are attributed a certain role. And you said that this role -- you said this in response to a question from my colleague. You said that this role meant that you had to go there. You gave them a speech, you told them that Prozor and Vakuf were in danger and that they were needed. And, finally, as far as I understood the matter, they accepted to go, they agreed to go, and they placed themselves under the authority of Colonel Siljeg. Is that, in fact, the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In essence, yes. General Petkovic is a high-ranking professional officer in the JNA. He has issued thousands of perfect orders. The fact that this one isn't a perfect order shows that we weren't dealing with an army in which orders are issued in the usual way. He was aware of the fact that men and units refused to obey orders for many reasons, and that is why item 4 says: "Do realise that ..." item 2 says report to Praljak, and because I knew the men, I knew half of them very well -- well, because that, they would go and he'd be informed of it. They arrived. I spoke to them, I went into the field with them. I -- Siljeg was there, too, and they were incorporated within the normal chain of command. What can I do? That's what the army was like. It's not my fault that I or, rather, Petkovic didn't have the 101st American Marine Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what you say, there's a small issue. Look at the stamp next to the signature of General Petkovic. You see there number 2, a number "2" on the stamp. As far as I know, General Petkovic was not the number 2. How come that there's the number "2" here? You're going to tell me, perhaps, that, I can't give you an answer. Well, tell me that you can't answer the question. When General Petkovic testifies, I will ask him. But as far as you are concerned, can you give me an answer? Tell me. It's not in the transcript unless you say it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us imagine that I am an officer in the HVO and I receive this order, and I am polarised by the stamps. I look at the order and I see that General Petkovic has the number 2. Can I legitimately ask myself whether number 1 is not Slobodan Praljak, especially so if I am familiar with the document on the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on that stamp, we don't see the Main Staff and everything. I don't know where it came from. On that one, you can't see everything. You can't see that it is the Main Staff at the bottom. And I think General Petkovic is very familiar with these things, and you will be able to ask him these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. When the time comes, we'll look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have the floor. We've exhausted --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've exhausted this issue and this document, in my submission, and I think it's time to move on. P03887, 3887. General, this one is dated the 2nd of August, 1993. We have a signature, "Ilija Franjic," who in this document is indicated to be the military police commander in Rama-Prozor at this time. Do you know whether, in fact, Mr. Franjic was the military police commander in Prozor on the 2nd of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed him to that position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Under the structure of the Military Police Administration, would he have been appointed to that position by Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in this document Mr. Franjic is issuing what he calls an approval regarding freedom of movement, and he says that: "In the capacity of the Rama-Prozor Military Police commander, I personally grant Omer Beric, aka Baja, born on the 2nd of March, 1940...," et cetera, "... a member of the HVO and of the HDZ, freedom of movement throughout the Rama municipality, having all the rights that are enjoyed by all other members of the Croatian ethnicity." Before I continue, General, would you agree with me that based on his name, it would appear that Omer Beric was a Muslim person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could make such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then the document continues: "I also strictly forbid any harassment of the above-mentioned or belittling of his integrity in any other way. "The above-mentioned is bound to report to the military police commander or his deputy on a daily basis. "This approval regarding freedom of movement for the above-mentioned is valid indefinitely or until it is revoked." Now, General, what we have here is a person who appears to be of Muslim ethnicity, who's a member of the HVO armed forces, because a military identification card is indicated, and he's also a member of the party, the Croatian Democratic Unit, the HDZ. The first question would be, General, whether you're aware of this particular situation or similar situations in which these sorts of freedom of movement documents were issued to Muslim people in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because at this period of time, you're commander of the HVO Main Staff, and as we've been discussing, this is taking place right within the area that you spent most of your time and directed most of your attention, Prozor; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this happened in the area where I was, but on the 2nd of August, as far as I am concerned, there was so much shooting along a line 30 kilometres long that apart from defending the front-lines, there was nothing else in my mind, nor could there be, from night to night, one night to the next, from one day to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me, based on the fact that you were in this region, that it was necessary to issue this sort of document because members of the Muslim population in Prozor, even by August of 1993, were being terrorised and victimised by the HVO; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with this order, but I did not see, nor did I have any knowledge about the Muslims being terrorised, not the least information about that. On the contrary, I had some contacts with the hodja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to put this to you. We talked last week -- or we talked about an autonomous Croatian area that you wanted. Let me put this to you, that when the sort of thing that's referenced here, where it's necessary to issue passes to people of one ethnicity, directing that they have all the rights to be enjoyed or that are enjoyed by members of another ethnicity, that's the sort of situation that happens when you start carving out territories based on ethnicity; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you, sir. The strength of the attack, the number of people from Bugojno, the dispersed army, the crimes of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, may be the reason for this kind of wording, that you mustn't act against them. The number of dead HVO people was very high in those days as a result of attacks by the BH Army, so I can't comment on what Mr. Franjic wrote there. But to have control over those people and the 15.000 refugees and one and a half thousand combatants, the situation was extremely difficult. You don't have an apparatus to deal with it. It's mostly talk, talk, talk, and persuasion as to what may be done under what -- and what may not. Of course, there were things that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But the fact is that every Muslim in Prozor was entitled to this sort of treatment, equal treatment, not just Muslims who happened to be carrying HVO or HDZ membership cards; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the military police in Prozor should have been protecting all of the people, including Muslims, regardless of whether they were members of the HVO or carried HDZ membership cards. Would you agree with me there, too?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that too, sir, but the military police was mainly involved at the front, both the military and the civilian police, because the BH Army was conducting a terrible aggression. These are facts. And I suppose Franjic wanted to emphasise that you must treat him like a Croat, not to distinguish between them, but the people who had left dozens of dead and captured members up in Bugojno -- you see, reprisals are a terrible thing. Of course, that is a crime, there's no doubt about it, but -- we know that it's a criminal offence, but still people do all kinds of things. And we know that this was a terribly difficult time for anyone, and one would -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document, unless there's a question on this one, Mr. President, the next document is P03458, 3458. This is going back a few weeks to the 15th of July. This is a report of SIS Chief Drago Banovic of the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone SIS, and it's a report to the SIS Administration, HZ-HB, Mostar. And he's reporting that the military security situation in Prozor has been disturbed by members of the local military police, or civilian police, or members of the Rama Brigade. And he says that: "In Prozor, the military police is the strongest by numbers, with 134 military policemen, who do not answer to anyone for their 'work,' who raid villages, loot, torch, and so on. We have pointed to the problems with the above-mentioned several times already, but nothing has been done on the matter." And then he goes on to cite a specific example of an event that occurred on the 5th of July, where houses were burned, stock was killed, and we see the rest. He continues, and I'm moving to the next page now in the English: "They are taking from the Muslims gold, money, and more valuable goods which are ending up in the pockets of local thieves (mostly military policemen, whose commander knows about them but is not doing anything). Many more examples could be cited." Now, General, the first question is this, because we're going to talk about the military police and the military police that you were using when you were in Prozor: The fact is, first of all, that the looting and the theft and the terrorising of the Muslim population that we've been talking about, as early as October of 1992, the fact is, General, it was continuing here in Prozor in the months that followed here, as late as the 15th of July; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I expected to reply, that I knew about all this and did nothing? This is a report I have nothing to do with. These are reports that have nothing to do with me. It's a report signed by Mr. Banovic, and you're asking me to testify about it as if I knew that the situation was like he says. I've told you what I was aware of, what I did, and I would stop there. Mr. Stringer, you could have spoken to Mr. Banovic and brought him here to tell him -- to ask him about the connections, rather than asking me about things that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You spent August and September of 1993 in Prozor. I recognise this is from 15 July, but the fact is, General, and this is my question: You were aware, weren't you, in August of 1993, that the Muslim population was being preyed upon by the military police in Prozor? You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not. And I didn't spend the whole of August and September in Prozor. I spent some time going to Mostar. On the 15th, I was involved in battles in the south of Mostar. When I say "most of the time," then you mustn't take that to mean for two months without interruption, because I was also on the hills and to the south of Mostar. But I did spend a good part of the time down there fighting. Unfortunately, fighting on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you're fighting. You're the commander of the HVO military -- excuse me, the HVO Main Staff, and you're fighting. Are you telling us, General, that because you're busy fighting, you can legitimately avoid undertaking all of the other responsibilities that fall to the highest-ranking member of the HVO military, responsibilities such as looking after civilian populations in areas under the command of you and your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian population was not under my command, and I am not responsible for the civilian population. Other people are responsible for that. Secondly, sir, one has 24 hours at one's disposal, and responsibility doesn't stem -- does stem from the situation one is in. You cannot be held responsible for something -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we're going to end in just a minute, because I know that there's a matter to bring up, but let me just conclude with this. Yesterday, you told us that you didn't have any responsibility or you bore no responsibility for HVO prisoners of war during the time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff. Now you're telling us that in addition to that, you bear no responsibility -- you have no obligations in respect of civilians who find themselves within zones under HVO military control? Is that your testimony as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is a military zone? I am not an occupier. I didn't occupier a certain territory or a captured territory, and then to administer that territory. A military commander has the defence lines, and the territory behind him is not under his command, as far as I am familiar with international war law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you're only responsible for what is happening on the front-line and you're not responsible, as the commander, for the general area that's controlled by the HVO military behind the front-lines; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you saying that the HVO military is holding behind the lines? The HVO is holding the lines. It has a narrow belt behind it, and it is not controlling the Rama municipality because the positions towards the army are in Uskoplje. The Rama municipality is not a military zone, it's not an occupied area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we should come back to this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Kovacic, we have nine minutes exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall be very brief. In view of the schedule that has been distributed prior to the recess, let me remind you that we had envisaged that General Praljak's testimony, including the possible redirect, would be completed on Monday, the 31st of August, and that on the 1st of September we can call our first expert witness, our first witness, et cetera. Of course, I think that in the mail that we have sent, that we cannot envisage with precision how long the cross would take on the part of the Prosecution, and that, therefore, certain leeway must be allowed for in the schedule. I am in touch with my learned friend from the Prosecution regarding the schedule. We communicate very well. I am following the number of hours that he has used, but we both agree that it is very difficult to envisage when this cross-examination will be completed because the progress is rather atypical. I have analysed the amount of time used by the Prosecution compared with the overall time. It varies a lot, and it is very difficult to plan for the future. I have a clearly technical problem. It is quite clear that the Prosecution will not be finished at least by mid-week, so if, theoretically, the first day for the first expert is Thursday, the 3rd of September, I must tomorrow, by the latest, inform the Victims and Witnesses Unit for them to organise their trip. So what may happen is that the cross-examination may be completed, you, Your Honours, may also have certain additional questions. We do not think that the redirect will take more than one or two hours, but we cannot be sure. But I would like to avoid the situation when we finish our work and the witness isn't here. Then, also, there are certain obligations and funds involved. I can ask for the witness to be brought on the 2nd or the 3rd of September. I'm not paying him. It's the Registry that's paying. Of course, I can't do that. I'm trying to be reasonable, and I'm trying to bring the witness two or three days before his testimony for the minimum proofing that we need to do. At the same time, I do not wish to be in a situation that I could call a witness on Monday and I haven't called him in time. So could I please ask that perhaps tomorrow, at the end of the day, we try to make some forecasts. I know that it is difficult. Of course, the closer we are to the end, it will be easier, and my learned friend has agreed with me in that respect, but it's too vague for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, it is almost impossible to forecast, because the Prosecution have 16 hours. They have used 24 hours. They have 16 hours left. Mr. Stringer may tell us now whether he's going to use those 16 hours or not. A second factor that we know, and that is that you're going to use about two hours for the redirect. As far as I am concerned, I will be very brief. I will only have some questions to put to Mr. Praljak regarding the maps, because I wish to see the exact positions of the units over time. This will not take long. But the other Defence counsels may also have questions to put. The Chamber is not opposed to this, but having deliberated, the members of the Chamber feel that if Madam Alaburic has questions to put -- but this will be taken off her time. But we don't know at this stage whether she intends to have questions or not. I'm talking about the Stojic Defence. So, first of all, it's up to Mr. Stringer to tell us how much time he intends to use, because he still has 16 hours to his credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's really hard for me to say whether the Prosecution will use the entire 16 that's left or not. What's easier for me to think about is the topics and the binders that we have completed versus the topics and the binders that are left, and that's -- all of us can look on the list that we filed prior to the beginning of the proceedings last week, and I would have to take a look to see. So for me, we are intending to question the general on all the topics that are set out in that list. If it takes us 16 hours to do it, then that's what we're going to do. I would be delighted if it took less than the full 40 hours, Mr. President, I can assure you, but at this stage it's really -- I wouldn't want to say about the hours. What I can say is about the lists and the topics that remain. And as I've been communicating with counsel for General Praljak, what we are going to be doing is we're going to be informing them, you know, when there are four binders left, and then three binders, and then two, which is for me, at least at the moment, a more accurate way of giving an idea of how the pace is going, as opposed to trying to anticipate whether we'll use the full 40 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In any event, what appears to be already more or less certain is that your witness, Mr. Kovacic, will not come next Monday because we won't be finished by next Monday. So it's better to see where we stand mid-week. Perhaps we will have a clearer idea maybe next Wednesday, and then we will see how we stand. But he certainly won't be coming on Monday, so it would be best for you to raise this issue next Wednesday. Perhaps we will have a better idea then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I fully agree with this methodology that as we approach the end, it's easier to judge when this will be over. But for technical reasons, we have to give instructions to the Victims and Witness Unit a minimum seven years [as interpreted] in advance. We have told the witnesses roughly when they're expected, but that's as much as we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Seven years in advance?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, seven days. My mistake, the interpreter's mistake, sorry. Seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, seven days. [Interpretation] Please bear in mind we will all know better in a couple of days, but don't crucify me if I'm a day late with the witness. But we will see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite normal, and no one will blame you for this because everyone knows that court schedules are difficult. But it's very good that Mr. Stringer and Mr. Kovacic are communicating amongst themselves, as you have told us, and this will help us to see things more clearly. So if you agree, we will raise the issue against next Wednesday. I think Judge Prandler wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I really feel duty-bound to state the following: that I would like to appeal to everyone in the "pretoir" [phoen] to exercise self-control in the forthcoming days in order to really let the Prosecution finish its business. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We meet again tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00, as you know, and we will finish at 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of August, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
